content: Hepatitis A, also known as infectious hepatitis, is a widespread epidemic disease. Immunoglobulins are used for passive immunization as a preventive measure against this condition. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the benefits and potential harms of using immunoglobulins for both pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis in preventing hepatitis A. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Chinese Biomedical Database, and the Science Citation Index Expanded. The search included trials published up until October 2008. Additionally, reference lists of identified publications were reviewed, and three journals were manually searched for relevant studies. The inclusion criteria for this analysis were randomized clinical trials that investigated the use of immunoglobulin prophylaxis for preventing hepatitis A. These trials were included regardless of their blinding status, publication status, or language. Data extraction was performed by two authors and verified by a third author. The results were expressed as relative risks (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The primary outcome of interest was the occurrence of hepatitis A. A total of 13 trials involving 567,476 participants were included in the analysis. These participants were randomized to receive either pre-exposure or post-exposure prophylaxis. However, the trials were found to have a high risk of bias and were heterogeneous in terms of study settings, participant characteristics, interventions, and outcome measures. The meta-analysis of six randomized trials demonstrated that immunoglobulins used for pre-exposure prophylaxis significantly reduced the incidence of hepatitis A in adults over a follow-up period of 6 to 12 months. Specifically, 1,020 cases of hepatitis A occurred among 286,503 individuals who received immunoglobulins, compared to 761 cases among 134,529 individuals in the control group (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.70; random-effects model). Similarly, four trials showed a significant reduction in hepatitis A cases among children aged 3 to 17 years over the same follow-up period. In this group, 917 cases occurred among 210,822 children who received immunoglobulins, compared to 677 cases among 78,960 children in the control group (RR 0.45; 95% CI 0.34 to 0.59). When comparing different doses of immunoglobulins, higher doses were generally more effective in preventing hepatitis A. For example, a dose of 1.5 ml was more effective than 0.75 ml, and 0.75 ml was more effective than 0.1 ml. Importantly, no significant systemic adverse events were reported in the trials. One trial specifically evaluated the use of immunoglobulins for post-exposure prophylaxis and found that immunoglobulins were more effective than placebo in preventing hepatitis A. However, when comparing immunoglobulins to the inactivated hepatitis A vaccine, there was no significant difference in seroconversion rates to hepatitis A vaccine antibodies at four weeks (RR 1.16; 95% CI 0.98 to 1.38). Nevertheless, immunoglobulins were significantly less effective than the vaccine in achieving higher antibody levels at 8, 12, or 24 weeks. In conclusion, immunoglobulins appear to be effective for both pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis of hepatitis A. However, the positive findings should be interpreted with caution due to the limited number of trials, the time period in which the studies were conducted, and the high risk of bias in the included trials. Further rigorous and well-designed trials are warranted to confirm these findings.
